summary:
We developed Mars Navigator, a free map and survival guide for the first astronauts on Mars. Mars has no GPS, no magnetic compass, freezing nights and strong radiation, and a message to Earth can take up to 22 minutes, so crews must find their way safely.

Built on NASA Mars Trek imagery, Curiosity’s real drive path and official Mars place names, our map lets a crew pick a mission: land, find water ice, search for life, power the base, stay safe or take a Marswalk. The map then switches on the right NASA data and shows a checklist. A temperature clock marks every hour GO, CAUTION or NO-GO. Routes can be walked, driven by rover or flown in a nuclear-powered aircraft, with turn-by-turn arrows. A 3D globe shows the Sun’s position and Earth’s distance, and a safety layer marks radiation shelters and dust storm alerts.

It matters because safe movement is the first survival skill on Mars. The app runs offline at a Mars base, so crews never depend on Earth to know where they are and when to turn back. Next, we want to add data from the UAE’s Hope probe to make our temperature clock more accurate.
details:
What it does and how it works

Mars Navigator is a free website / APP that helps the first crews on Mars decide where to walk, when to walk and how to stay safe. It opens on a map of Gale Crater, where Curiosity landed.

The App helps multiple teams at a time and has in-built team communication within Mars and also with Earth. It can allow team to take images, videos - upload in real time so that MAP can be improved.

App starts by

  • Pick a mission: land and set up base, find water ice, search for signs of life, power the base, stay safe, or take a daily Marswalk. The map flies there, turns on the right NASA layers and shows a checklist.
  • NASA Mars Trek maps: Viking colour, MOLA height, THEMIS day and night heat, sharper CTX and HiRISE photos, dust cover, buried ice, landing sites and 434 official place names.
  • A temperature clock, fitted to Curiosity and Perseverance weather data, marks every hour GO, CAUTION or NO-GO. Leave at 10:30, turn back by 14:30, be inside by 15:30.
  • Routes follow the path Curiosity really drove, with a blinking turn-by-turn arrow, time and distance left, and a compass. Travel on foot (about 2 km/h), by rover (about 10 km/h) or by a nuclear-powered Navigator aircraft (about 350 km/h, based on NASA-funded studies).
  • A safety layer marks natural radiation shelters such as cliffs and caves, and gives dust storm alerts.
  • A 3D globe shows the Sun’s real position, sunrise and sunset, what lies in each direction, a suit meter and how far away Earth is today.
  • Crew chat and a field camera on every page let teams share messages and geotagged photos.
  • A Field Guide explains the science, and a presentation with three narrated presenters explains the project in 30 seconds, 1 minute or 2 minutes.

Benefits
Mars has no GPS and no magnetic compass, and a message to Earth can take up to 22 minutes. Our map lets a crew plan and move safely on its own, without waiting for Mission Control.

Intended impact
Fewer risky walks, faster decisions and more time for science on the first human missions. On Mars the app would run offline from the base computer with all maps loaded, so suits, rovers and tablets reach it over a local radio link, and orbiters relay photos to Earth. Today it also teaches students how real NASA data can keep people safe.

Tools, languages and software
HTML, CSS and JavaScript; Leaflet for the map and three.js for the 3D globe; NASA Mars Trek map tiles; the Mars24 method for Sun position; Kokoro text-to-speech for the narration; Python and ffmpeg to prepare audio and video. It is hosted free on GitHub Pages and works on any phone, tablet or computer browser, with no special hardware.


How it is creative

  • The temperature-zone clock turns weather data into a simple GO, CAUTION or NO-GO rule for every hour.
  • Routes reuse ground that a rover has already proven safe to cross.
  • Natural cliffs and caves become radiation shelters.
  • Two solar power plans: three farms on the equator so one is always in daylight, or one farm at the north pole with panels that turn like sunflowers.
  • Animated presenters explain everything in a child-friendly way.

    Next step: the UAE’s Hope probe
    We built Mars Navigator in the UAE, which has its own Mars mission. Hope measures the atmosphere across the whole planet, through the day and the seasons, so it is the data we would like to add next to make our temperature clock more accurate. We have not used Hope data in this version.

Factors our team considered

  • Safety first: cold, radiation, dust storms and getting back before dark.
  • Radio delay and no internet on Mars, so the app must work offline.
  • Accuracy: every number comes from a named NASA or partner source; estimates and simulated suit readings are clearly marked.
  • Ease of use: plain words, big buttons, a colour legend, and layouts for phone, tablet and computer.
  • Fair credit: every image, dataset and tool is credited on the Team & Sources page.

Team
A Team of Year 5 Students from Winchester School, Jebel Ali, Dubai. Parts of the project, field guide, temperature zones, navigation and route planning; a safety layer of radiation, shelters and dust storms; and a solar power plan.

We also took feedback from other senior students, teachers... below is their feedback in their own words and we adapted a few changes basis their feedback

Anonymous SENIOR Student from Winchester School

1. Was it easy to find what to do?

Answer: It was indeed easy to find the tools and the drop down option help a lot to keep the search focused.

2. Did the GO, CAUTION and NO-GO colours make sense?

Answer: Color coding really helps in giving a visual interpretation though, we could align the color schema similar to regular google maps colors so while GO continues to be GREEN, CAUTION continues to be RED, but NO-GO can use BROWN/BLACK colors.

3. What was the best part?

Answer: I liked the route planner simulation. It gives very good simulation, while selecting the mode of transport along with clear go or no-go or caution as per the times.

4. What was confusing or hard?

Answer: The mission selection could be more easily worded and clear for easy selection.

5. What would you change:

Answer: We may remove the time of stay at an end point as currently we are showing one way travel only. As a next step, we may wish to draw the route map through the "go" zones only and may suggest stop-overs in case there are no continuous "go" zones which may need some time to pass before next step turns "go" with time.



Anonymous School Student of Winchester:

1. Was it easy to find what to do?

Answer: I tried finding out the Stay sage: radiation and dust, thinking that it could be a daily marswalk so that confused me a bit.

2. Did the GO, CAUTION and NO-GO colours make sense?

Answer: The colors are ok but the route could also show the go sections of the route as the slider is moved so that astronaut can plan their travel.

3. What was the best part?

Answer: My favorite part is the google earth kind of visualization of Mars surface along with option of Altimeter version, temperature version both day time and night time.

4. What was confusing or hard?

Answer: I am confused on how the astronaut actually check where they are and which direction they need to move now? Are they referencing to the Mars station for getting relative direction, position?

5. What would you change:

Answer: Having a set-up similar to google maps would make it really nice.
